supplement.where: PDF pp. 44-118: Appendices A-G, with Appendix G ending on PDF p. 117 and appendix references on PDF p. 118. Full survey flows for the other conditions are available upon request (PDF p. 44, Appendix A).
supplement.holds: Included appendix tables supply arm means, SDs, pairwise differences and SEs (A.3, D.1, G.2), robustness analyses (A.4-A.5, F.2-F.4), attrition (F.1), additional output measures (D.2, D.5, E.5-E.8, F.5), and problem-statement similarity tests (Figure E.1). Appendix C gives coding rubrics and classifier validation; Appendix F documents preregistration changes. Appendix G does not identify the follow-up outcome coder.

paper_design_summary: The main experiment individually randomized 338 MBA students in a core strategy course to no LLM, GPT-4 from ideation onward, or GPT-4 from problem formulation onward; 305 were analyzed after 33 absences (PDF pp. 13, 105; Tables 1 and F.1 on PDF pp. 37, 107). Participants formulated a business-case problem, generated options and selected one, with submitted outputs scored for fluency, category coverage, contextual detail, strategic composition and similarity across participants. A separate executive-education follow-up randomized GPT-4o access timing at the team level and analyzed 96 people in 24 teams working on their own strategic challenges (PDF pp. 26, 112, 117).

studies.label: Main experiment: MBA students, Rated case (individual)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Timing of access to a GPT-4-based LLM: none (control), from ideation onward (partial treatment), or from problem formulation onward (full treatment)
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to three experimental groups, stratified by their section, gender, and a binary indicator of whether their last job was in consulting.
assignment.prereg_locator: PDF p. 1 (title page note: 'pre-registered on the AEA RCT registry'); PDF p. 14 (printed p. 13), Section 3.1; PDF p. 105 (printed appendix p. 62), Appendix F. No registry ID is printed.

arms.name: Full treatment

arms.name: Partial treatment

participants.exclusions: The preregistration anticipated 336 students; two students initially categorized as partners were subsequently included, bringing the assigned sample to 338. Of these, 305 were analyzed and 33 were absent (PDF p. 105, Appendix F; PDF p. 107, Table F.1). Assigned counts by arm are not reported. Analyzed arm counts are Full 102, Partial 100, Control 103 (PDF pp. 13, 37, 55). Duration-outlier exclusion analyzed N = 293 (PDF p. 57, Table A.4); excluding the two additions analyzed N = 303 (PDF p. 107, Table F.2). The analysis excludes absentees and is not a full intention-to-treat analysis, despite the authors terminology.
participants.who: MBA students in a core strategy course, four classroom sections; mean age 30, 32% female, 31% previously in management consulting
participants.quote: Our sample for the main experiment consists of 305 MBA students enrolled in a core strategy course at a leading business school.
participants.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 10), Section 3.1; PDF p. 13, assignment and analyzed arm counts; PDF p. 37, Table 1; PDF p. 55, Table A.1; PDF p. 105, Appendix F; PDF p. 107, Table F.1

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4-based LLM: standard ChatGPT web interface in sections 1-2; custom wrapper on OpenAI's API (gpt-4) pre-loaded with the case in sections 3-4
ai_tool.how_used: Free chat during assigned stages; all participants, including the control group, received optional suggested prompts (PDF pp. 13-14, Section 3.1; PDF p. 55, Table A.2). The custom-wrapper sections produced interaction logs for 88 participants. The fine-tuned GPT-3.5 Turbo classifier was used to score outputs, not as the experimental assistance tool (PDF pp. 15, 70).

task.description: Pre-distributed business case (Rated, an unprofitable online reviews platform). Participants (i) articulated the strategic reasons for low profitability (problem formulation), (ii) submitted strategic options one at a time, as many as they wished, and (iii) selected the best option. Done individually in class via an online survey with sequential stage instructions.
task.duration: Mean 44.39 minutes (SD 15.29) for the whole task (PDF p. 14, printed p. 13)

outcomes.name: Similarity of problem statements to the group centroid (convergence in problem framing)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Problem-formulation text embedded with bert-base-uncased (mean of last hidden layer); cosine similarity of each participant's embedding to the median embedding of their arm. Higher = more alike = less diverse (sign reversed relative to diversity). Only the full arm had AI at the problem-formulation stage; partial and control wrote problem statements without AI, so the control-vs-partial K-S p = 0.68 is not an AI contrast.

contrasts.reported: Figure E.1 density only; Full vs Partial K-S test p-value 0.063. Text: 'Problem statements in the full treatment groups were more similar to one another than in the partial treatment group (Appendix Figure E.1, K-S Test p = 0.063)'. No means or SEs printed. Direction coded for diversity (lower diversity in full arm).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 78 (printed appendix p. 35), Figure E.1; PDF p. 21 (printed p. 20), Section 5.1

contrasts.reported: Figure E.1: Control vs Full K-S test p-value 0.132. No direction stated in text; no means printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 78, Figure E.1

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity between each participant's problem-statement embedding and the arm's median embedding (centroid); compared as distributions
diversity_detail.embedding_model: bert-base-uncased, mean of last hidden layer over tokens
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each output against its own arm's centroid (median embedding)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests on one similarity score per participant. Only p-values and densities are reported; the K-S statistic, means, SDs, SEs and confidence intervals are not reported. Scores share an estimated arm centroid; participant-independent precision is not established.
diversity_detail.notes: Each participant contributes one problem statement. Higher similarity is coded as lower diversity. Only the Full arm had AI at this stage, so Full versus Partial is ai_vs_bau. This is an exploratory mechanism outcome (PDF pp. 21, 78), not a rated creativity outcome or an after-AI test.

outcomes.name: Proportion of broad (versus specific) options
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Few-shot classifier: BERT base (uncased) embeddings, each option assigned to the nearer of 'broad' and 'specific' centroids built from six hand-written anchor sentences (Table D.3); share of broad options per participant. Embeddings are averaged over the last hidden layer and class assignment uses Euclidean distance (PDF p. 76, Appendix D.2). The text reports partial-treatment p = 0.1, whereas Table D.5 prints 0.10** (0.04), with ** defined as p < 0.05 (PDF p. 77). Both are preserved; the exact partial-treatment p-value cannot be resolved from this PDF. Table D.4 defines broad versus specific articulation by the level of contextual detail in an option (PDF p. 77), so the construct is elaboration. Higher broadness means less elaboration. Directions for the AI-versus-control contrasts are therefore coded treatment_lower for elaboration; all reported coefficients, standard errors, and p-value claims remain exactly as printed on the broadness scale.

eligibility.reason: S1 meets all three criteria independently. Individuals were randomly assigned to GPT-4 access from problem formulation, access from ideation, or no AI (PDF p. 13, Section 3.1; individual assignment unit on PDF p. 16, Section 3.3). The study analyzed 305 people: Full 102, Partial 100, Control 103 (PDF p. 37, Table 1), after 33 absences from 338 assigned (PDF p. 105, Appendix F; PDF p. 107, Table F.1). The task instructions asked for creative, relevant business options (PDF p. 55, Table A.2), and submitted outputs were scored for fluency, within-participant category coverage, contextual detail and across-participant similarity (PDF p. 16, Section 3.2; PDF pp. 76-78, Appendix D.2 and Figure E.1; PDF pp. 84, 91-92, Appendix E.2.1 and Tables E.5-E.6). S1-O8 is flexibility and S1-O9 is elaboration; broadness has the inverse direction to elaboration. AI was available during ideation in both treatment arms and during problem formulation only in Full (PDF p. 13). S2 also meets the criteria through randomized AI configurations at the team level, 96 analyzed people in 24 teams, and option counts on team outputs (PDF pp. 26, 112, 117, Section 5.5, Appendix G and Table G.2). Both original experiments are field_rct under the codebook coursework definition. Strategic composition remains other; eligibility does not depend on unresolved scorers or the exact significance of the broadness result.

one_line_finding: Among 305 analyzed MBA students, GPT-4 raised option counts by 1.55 (SE 0.43) with full access and 2.68 (SE 0.55) with ideation-onward access, while full access lowered the strategic share by 0.07 (SE 0.03) and strategic selection by 0.15 (SE 0.07), with no clear partial-access effect on either strategic outcome (PDF p. 38, Table 2).

Appendix D.2 partial-treatment p = 0.1 conflicts with Table D.5 ** (p < 0.05); retain both printed claims.
Assigned counts by arm for the main experiment are not reported and remain null.
notes: Read the entire markdown conversion, including appendices and references, and verified recorded quantitative results against PDF text. No effect sizes were computed. Per form-spec rule 7, the outcomes arrays contain 15 main outcomes; IDs retain B's numbering. Secondary outcomes omitted from those arrays, but confirmed and retained here: S1 exit counts (PDF p. 110, Table F.5 col. 3), Full -0.13*** (0.04), Partial -0.12*** (0.04), control mean 0.16, N = 305, F = 0.52, p = 0.472; S1 change-pricing counts (same table col. 2), Full -0.14* (0.08), Partial -0.01 (0.09), control mean 0.52, N = 305, F = 2.55, p = 0.111. Both use the fine-tuned GPT-3.5 classifier described in Appendix C (PDF p. 70); exit and change-pricing were already present in both raw forms, combined in A and separated in B. The preregistered best-chosen exit/expand indicator differs from the exit count actually reported (PDF pp. 105, 110). S2 continue outcomes (PDF p. 117, Table G.2), N = 12 teams per arm: count Full 1.92 (SD 1.68), Partial 1.83 (SD 1.34), printed b = 0.08, se = 0.62, p = 0.894; proportion Full 0.39 (SD 0.34), Partial 0.40 (SD 0.29), b = -0.01, se = 0.13, p = 0.947; coding method is unknown (measure = null). Additional output variants not given separate records include continuation share and selection (Table D.2), average options per category (Table E.6 and Table 5), per-category indicators (Tables E.5-E.6), other problem-option overlap measures (Tables E.7-E.8), and first/last or option-index strategic analyses (Table 6 cols. 6-7); the option-level model uses a participant random intercept (PDF p. 96). Time, math accuracy, self-reports, and similarity/copying relative to a participant's own LLM interaction are not creativity/diversity outcomes across people. The paper reports no obtained peer ratings of option quality (PDF p. 105). The saved version is dated 22 February 2026, not the 2025 search-record version; exact sample continuity is unverified. Statistical directions for other outcomes refer to the named measured quantity, not a claim that a strategic/operational composition is intrinsically more creative. Directions with p-values above 0.05 remain qualified by their printed tests; p = 0.000 is reproduced as printed, not interpreted as zero probability. Main regressions have strata fixed effects and robust participant-level SEs (PDF p. 16); two-arm regressions and three-arm Wald tests have distinct estimates/tests and are retained separately. The problem-centroid outcome uses common arm centroids and supplies no usable SE. The paper's primary-status labels are kept separate from any later Atlas primary-estimate selection. The main fluency result is the relevant direct creativity outcome; strategic composition measures do not become creativity ratings merely because they were primary in the paper. For across_people, Full versus Control is the available no-AI contrast; Full versus Partial also compares AI with no AI at the problem-formulation stage. No outcome is after_ai. Source inconsistencies: Appendix A.1 Panel (b) reverses the full/partial log-subsample totals relative to Section 3.1 and Table A.6 (PDF pp. 14, 55, 59); no retained core contrast depends on these log counts. Table G.2's difference-column heading conflicts with its printed signs (PDF p. 117). Appendix D.2's partial broadness p-value conflicts with Table D.5 (PDF pp. 76-77). Section 3.2 points to Appendix A for coding, but the coding appendix is C (PDF pp. 15, 70). No source statement establishes overlap with a different paper or external corporate involvement. Table F.5 exit-count constant is 0.13*** (0.05) (PDF p. 110). Gender coding and exact sample continuity with the earlier version remain unverified; these uncertainties do not affect eligibility. Reconciled on 2026-10-09. Finalized on 2026-10-09 after reading the complete markdown, including Appendices A-G and appendix references, and checking the challenged passages and retained quantitative results against PDF text. Applied both outcome-lens corrections: S1-O8 is flexibility; S1-O9 is elaboration with direction reversed from raw broadness. All printed contrast statistics are preserved. The eight distinct open items cover all open_questions and all six unresolved reconciliation differences; none affects eligibility. The included supplement and both original field_rct classifications were rechecked. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as the prior review history.
